newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian Zagrebacka ups dividend on 1996 profit.
newsitem.headline: Croatian Zagrebacka ups dividend on 1996 profit.

text.p: Zagrebacka Banka, one of two Croatian companies listed in London, on Tuesday released buoyant 1996 profit figures and said good results allowed it to raise its dividend to six German marks per ordinary share.

The increase still has to be approved by the annual meeting on June 10, but shareholders are widely expected to pass it, analysts said. Zagrebacka paid a per share equivalent of five marks on 1995 results.
It said it expected last year's group retained profit to be just under 186 million kuna ($30.5 million) compared with zero in 1995.
"The (parent) bank itself should have (a profit of) around 156 million kuna after tax and dividend payments," board member Davor Holjevac told Reuters but he gave no comparable 1995 figure.
Earlier on Tuesday, the group announced a pre-tax profit of 349 million kuna for last year, against a consolidated 143 million loss in 1995. It made no indication of net earnings.

Its announcement came on the heels of news that IBCA, the European credit rating agency, had assigned Zagrebacka its first ratings of BBB- long-term and short-term A3, reflecting its strength and leading market position.
Moody's Investors Service assigned its Ba1/Not Prime rating to the bank's long- and short-term deposits, while giving a Ba1 assessment for its prospective Eurobond issue.
Zagrebacka's ordinary shares closed 50 kuna higher at 1,850 on the Zagreb Stock Exchange before the figures reached the market, but were seen as rising on the back of the latest news.
Its 1/10 Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs) have since firmed to $33.12 each from $31.37 at the open on London's Seaq International.
The group comprises Zagrebacka Banka, another bank Pomorska Banka, insurer Adriatic Osiguranje and a holding company that takes care of investments in hoteliers.
Although Zagrebacka netted over 124 million kuna in 1995, the year was negative for the group, making a 184 million kuna loss after heavy writeoffs on holdings in the tourist trade.
In 1996, parent profit before taxation climbed 104 million kuna to 266 million. This was in spite of what it described as a "restrictive monetary policy".
The group balance sheet strengthened some 18 percent last year from 17.1 billion kuna at the end of 1995.
Growth in Zagrebacka Banka assets was slightly lower at 16 percent from a total of 16.2 billion in 1995.
It particularly noted a rise of 437 million marks in foreign currency savings, which allowed it to boost lending to retail clients 260 million marks.
New provisions formed in 1996 to cushion the group against potential losses were put at 246 million kuna, with the bank's own risk provisions at 305 million. There was no comparison with 1995.
"Provisions are dispersed over various segments of the economy and they are believed to provide sufficient covering against potential risks," Zagrebacka said but added:
"In spite of the balance sheet growth, capital adequacy remained at the previous year's level."

It explained this by the fact that capital gains from a sale of the bank's shares last year were transferred into reserves. At the end of 1996, Zagrebacka had about 25 percent foreign shareholders, it said.
The group's financial statements have been audited by KPMG according to international accounting standards for the sixth year in a row. ($ = 6.091 Croatian kuna)
